01.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tells of two men fishing with nets on the Jordan River. One went into a cave by the shore where fish gathered, the sun set, and in the dark he could not find the way out. His friend waited long enough to be sure he had died, then went and told the man's household. The next morning the sun rose, the man saw the opening, came out, and arrived home to find a great eulogy under way for him. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: how great are the words of the Sages, who ruled that if a man is lost in water with a visible end his wife may remarry, but if the water has no visible end she may not.
01.why: The discussion has just dealt with Rav Sheila, who let a wife remarry after her husband vanished in the lake of Samkei, then admitted his error because waves could carry a man out of sight. This incident shows why the Sages refuse to presume death when a man disappears in such water.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Tells the incident and draws the lesson from it.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great collection of Jewish law. The Gemara often quotes one to support or challenge a point.

A body of water whose shores can all be seen from where the man went under. If he does not come up, witnesses would have seen him climb out somewhere, so his death can be presumed. In water with no visible end he might have come out unseen.

02.note: Rabban Gamliel recalls traveling on a boat and seeing another boat break apart and sink. He grieved for the Torah scholar aboard, Rabbi Akiva. But when Rabban Gamliel reached dry land, Rabbi Akiva came, sat down and debated Jewish law before him. Asked who had brought him up, Rabbi Akiva said a plank from the ship came to him, and he bowed his head to every wave that came at him. From this, the Sages said that when wicked people come upon a person he should bow his head before them. Rabban Gamliel said that at that moment he thought: how great are the words of the Sages, who said a wife may remarry when her husband is lost in water with a visible end, but not when the water has no end.
02.why: The Gemara has just rejected Rav Ashi's idea that a Torah scholar's survival would surely become known, ruling that no one lost in endless water is presumed dead. This is one of several accounts of men seen lost at sea who came back alive.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Tells the story; he watched the ship sink and later met the survivor.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Torah scholar on the sinking ship, who survived by clinging to a plank.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great collection of Jewish law.
Jewish law. To deliberate about halakha is to debate legal questions, as students did before their teachers.
A body of water whose shores cannot all be seen. A man who goes under there might come out somewhere unseen, so the Sages do not let his wife remarry on the assumption that he drowned.

03.note: Rabbi Akiva recalls traveling on a boat and seeing another boat tossed and sinking at sea. He grieved for the Torah scholar aboard, Rabbi Meir. But when Rabbi Akiva landed in the province of Cappadocia, Rabbi Meir came, sat down and debated Jewish law before him. Asked who had brought him up, Rabbi Meir said one wave tossed him to the next, and that one to the next, until a wave threw him up onto dry land. Rabbi Akiva said that at that moment he thought: how great are the words of the Sages, who said a wife may remarry when her husband is lost in water with a visible end, but not when the water has no end.
03.why: This follows Rabban Gamliel's account of Rabbi Akiva surviving a shipwreck, as a second case of a man seen lost at sea who came back alive, backing the rule that a wife may not remarry when her husband vanished in endless water.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells the story; he saw the ship sink and later met the survivor in Cappadocia.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Torah scholar on the sinking ship, carried ashore by the waves.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great collection of Jewish law.
A body of water whose shores cannot all be seen. A man who goes under there might come out somewhere unseen, so the Sages do not let his wife remarry on the assumption that he drowned.

04.note: The daughter of Neḥunya the well digger fell into the Great Cistern, and people came to tell Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa. After the first hour he told them: peace. After the second: peace. After the third: she has come up. He asked the girl who had pulled her up, and she said a ram came by, with an old man leading it. They asked Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa whether he was a prophet. He answered with the verse 'I am not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet,' and explained his reasoning: could the children of a righteous man come to harm through the very work he labors at?
04.why: The mishna cited Rabbi Meir's case of a man who came out of the Great Cistern alive after three days, and the Sages objected that miracles are not used to set law. The Gemara then tells of another rescue from the same cistern; right after, Rabbi Abba notes that Neḥunya's son still died of thirst.

people.name: Neḥunya the well digger
people.about: Father of the girl; Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa calls him righteous for his work digging water sources.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
people.about: The Sage the people turn to; he tells them hour by hour that the girl is safe, and then that she is out.

terms.meaning: A large cistern for storing water, also named in the mishna's earlier case of a man who fell into it.

05.note: A gentile went around calling out: Who is from the house of Ḥivvai? Who is from the house of Ḥivvai? Ḥivvai has died. On the strength of this, Rav Yosef allowed Ḥivvai's wife to marry. Another gentile went around saying: Alas for the brave horseman who was in Pumbedita, for he is dead. Rav Yosef, and some say Rava, allowed his wife to marry.
05.why: The mishna says a gentile who intends to testify is not believed. After learning that the Rabbis rejected Rabbi Oshaya's wider use of gentile testimony, the Gemara asks when a gentile is ever believed, and answers: when he speaks offhandedly, as in these two cases.

people.name: Ḥivvai
people.about: A man reported dead by a gentile calling out in the street.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who allowed the wives to remarry on the gentiles' reports.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Named in one version as the Sage who ruled in the horseman's case.

terms.meaning: Mentioning something in passing, with no aim of giving testimony or affecting a court's decision. A gentile's report of a death is believed only when said this way.
The first great written collection of Jewish law; the Gemara is the long discussion built around it.

06.note: A gentile went around calling: Who is from the house of Ḥasa? Ḥasa has drowned. Rav Naḥman exclaimed: By God! The fish have eaten Ḥasa. Because of what Rav Naḥman said, Ḥasa's wife went and married, and no one said anything to her. Rav Ashi learned from this that a remarriage after a husband vanished in water with no visible end is not undone once it has happened. Others tell it differently: Rav Naḥman actually allowed her to marry, reasoning that Ḥasa was a great man, so if he had come out alive the news would have spread. The Gemara rejects that reasoning: great man or not, the marriage stands after the fact but is not allowed beforehand.
06.why: It continues the cases of a gentile's offhand report of a death. Here the man drowned, so the case also tests the rule that a wife may not remarry when her husband vanished in endless water.

people.name: Ḥasa
people.about: A man reported drowned by a gentile; called a great man in one version.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage whose exclamation, or in another version his ruling, led to Ḥasa's wife remarrying.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Draws the legal lesson from the case.

terms.meaning: From the outset, before the act. Something not allowed ab initio may still be allowed to stand after the fact, once it has been done.
A body of water whose shores cannot all be seen. A man who goes under there might come out unseen, so his death is not presumed.

07.note: A gentile told a Jew: Cut fodder and give it to my animals on Shabbat, or I will kill you as I killed so-and-so the Jew, who would not cook me a pot of food on Shabbat. The dead man's wife heard this and came before Abaye. He put off her case through three pilgrim festivals. Rav Adda bar Ahava told her: Go to Rav Yosef, whose knife is sharp. She went, and Rav Yosef settled it from a teaching: a gentile selling fruit at market who says his fruit is forbidden produce has said nothing, since he only meant to make his goods look better. The translation explains that Rav Yosef therefore would not rely on the gentile's claim.
07.why: The Gemara has shown that a gentile who mentions a death offhandedly is believed. This case asks about a gentile who speaks for his own purposes, here to frighten someone.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The first Sage the widow asks; he delays his ruling through three festivals.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: Sends the woman on to Rav Yosef.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage 'whose knife is sharp', who resolves her case.

terms.meaning: Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. The translation notes that Sages gathered to study on these festivals, so a hard question could be raised before many of them.
Fruit from a tree's first three years of growth, which Jewish law forbids eating.
A figure of speech for a sharp legal mind who can cut through a hard question.

08.note: Abba Yudan of Sidon reports that a Jew and a gentile traveled the road together. Later the gentile came back and said: Alas for the Jew who was with me on the road, for he died on the way, and I buried him. On this statement, the Jew's wife was allowed to marry.
08.why: Rav Yosef has just refused to rely on a gentile who spoke with his own aims. This report gives the other side: a gentile who mentions a death in passing, in a lament, is believed, and the widow may remarry.

people.name: Abba Yudan of Sidon
people.about: Reports the incident.

09.note: A group of men chained together by collars was being marched to Antokhya. A gentile later came and said: Alas for the collared people, for they died, and I buried them. Their wives were allowed to marry. In another incident, sixty men were walking to the siege of Beitar. A gentile came and said: Alas for those sixty people walking on the road to Beitar, for they died, and I buried them. Their wives too were allowed to marry.
09.why: These continue Abba Yudan of Sidon's list of cases in which a gentile's passing lament over the dead was trusted enough to let the widows remarry.

terms.meaning: A collar. The translation explains these were prisoners, each chained by a collar around the neck.
A siege. Here, the siege of the city of Beitar.

10.note: A man came before Rabbi Tarfon to testify that a woman's husband had died. Asked how he knew, he said they were traveling together when a troop of soldiers chased them; the husband grabbed an olive branch, tore it off and drove the troop back. 'Lion, well done,' the witness said to him, and the husband asked how he knew his name was Lion: in his town he was called Yoḥanan son of Rabbi Yehonatan, the lion of Kefar Shiḥayya. Later he fell ill and died, and Rabbi Tarfon let the wife marry. In a second version the branch is a fig branch, and Rabbi Tarfon tests the witness by misstating the name. The witness corrects him, keeps his story straight two or three times, and only then does Rabbi Tarfon let the wife marry.
10.why: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Tarfon demands formal cross-examination of witnesses to a husband's death, since the second version has him question the witness and the first does not. It answers that the point is disputed: Rabbi Akiva says it is not needed, Rabbi Tarfon says it is.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The judge who hears the witness and allows the widow to marry.

people.name: Yoḥanan, son of Rabbi Yehonatan
people.about: The dead husband, known in his town as the lion; in the second version called Yoḥanan son of Yonatan.

terms.meaning: The formal cross-examination of witnesses that a court uses to test testimony, checking details for consistency.
Hebrew for lion. The witness used it as praise, and it turned out to be the man's nickname.

11.note: Rabbi Yosei recalls entering a ruin in Jerusalem to pray. Elijah came and guarded the entrance until he finished, then greeted him and asked why he had gone in. To pray, Rabbi Yosei said. Elijah said he should have prayed on the road; Rabbi Yosei feared travelers would interrupt him; Elijah said he should then have said the short prayer. Rabbi Yosei learned three things: not to enter a ruin, that one may pray on the road, and that on the road one says a short prayer. Elijah asked what he had heard there. A Heavenly voice cooing like a dove, he said: Woe, that I destroyed My house, burned My Temple and exiled My children. Elijah said it cries so three times a day, and that when Israel praises God's name in the synagogue, God laments the children exiled from their father's table.
11.why: Rav, as quoted just before, taught that God roars like a lion at each watch of the night over the Temple's destruction. Rabbi Yosei's account bears out that lament, and the Gemara then turns to why one may not enter a ruin.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Tells the story; he went into the ruin to pray.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who guards the entrance and then questions and teaches Rabbi Yosei.

terms.meaning: A short form of the central daily prayer, set for someone who cannot concentrate on the full version, such as a traveler on the road.
A voice from Heaven, heard by people, that speaks for God.
A prayer said in the synagogue; the congregation answers 'May His great name be blessed'.

12.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba fell ill. Rabbi Yoḥanan came to visit and asked him: Is your suffering dear to you? Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said: Neither the suffering nor its reward. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Give me your hand. He gave him his hand, and Rabbi Yoḥanan raised him up.
12.why: The Gemara is weighing which sufferings count as 'afflictions of love', sent by God out of love and bringing reward. Here a sick man says he wants neither the suffering nor its reward.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: The sick man; the translation calls him Rabbi Yoḥanan's student.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Visits him and raises him from his sickbed.

terms.meaning: The discussion holds that suffering accepted with love brings reward from God. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba would rather be spared both.

13.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan fell ill. Rabbi Ḥanina came to visit and asked him: Is your suffering dear to you? Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Neither the suffering nor its reward. Rabbi Ḥanina said: Give me your hand. He gave him his hand, and Rabbi Ḥanina raised him up.
13.why: It mirrors the story just told, in which Rabbi Yoḥanan healed his own student. The Gemara asks why he could not raise himself, and answers that a prisoner cannot free himself from prison.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The sick man here, though in the story before he healed another.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Visits Rabbi Yoḥanan and raises him from his sickbed.

14.note: Rabbi Elazar fell ill, and Rabbi Yoḥanan came to visit. Rabbi Elazar was lying in a dark room; Rabbi Yoḥanan bared his arm, and light shone from it. He saw Rabbi Elazar crying and asked why. If over Torah he had not learned enough, he said, it matters only that the heart is turned to Heaven; if over poverty, not everyone gets two tables; if over children, here is the bone of my tenth son. Rabbi Elazar said: I am crying over this beauty of yours that will rot in the earth. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Over that you surely should cry, and both of them wept. Meanwhile Rabbi Yoḥanan asked if his suffering was dear to him. Neither it nor its reward, he said. Give me your hand, said Rabbi Yoḥanan, and he raised him up.
14.why: It completes a series of sickbed visits in a discussion of 'afflictions of love'. Rabbi Yoḥanan's consolations go over the sufferings the Gemara has been sorting, and the bone of his tenth son was quoted earlier when it asked whether losing children counts.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The sick man, who weeps over Rabbi Yoḥanan's beauty; the translation calls him Rabbi Yoḥanan's student.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Visits, consoles and weeps with Rabbi Elazar, then raises him up.

terms.meaning: The translation explains this as wealth and Torah learning together; not everyone is granted both.

terms.term: the bone of my tenth son
terms.meaning: Earlier in the discussion the Gemara explains that Rabbi Yoḥanan lost ten children and kept a small bone of the tenth, which he showed to console others.

15.note: Four hundred barrels of Rav Huna's wine turned to vinegar. Rav Yehuda, brother of Rav Sala the Pious, came with the Sages (some say Rav Adda bar Ahava with the Sages) and told him to examine his deeds. Am I suspect in your eyes? he asked. They answered: Is God suspect of judging without justice? Rav Huna said: If anyone has heard something against me, say it. They had heard he did not give his tenant farmer his share of the vine cuttings. He steals everything from me, said Rav Huna. They answered with the saying: steal from a thief and you too get a taste of theft. Rav Huna took it on himself to give the share. Some say the vinegar turned back into wine; some say the price of vinegar rose until it sold at the price of wine.
15.why: It follows a series of stories about suffering. Here the loss is treated as a sign to examine one's conduct, and once the wrong is put right the loss is undone.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage whose wine soured and who is asked to examine his deeds.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Brother of Rav Sala the Pious; he and the Sages visit Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: Named in another version as the visitor in place of Rav Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A man who works another's land in return for a share of what it produces. The translation explains he was also owed a share of the vine cuttings.

16.note: A man prayed behind the synagogue without turning to face it. Elijah passed by and saw him, and appeared to him as an Arab. He said: Is this how you stand before your Master? Elijah drew a sword and killed him.
16.why: Rav Huna has just said that one who prays behind the synagogue is called wicked, and Abaye limited this to one who does not turn his face toward it. This man is exactly that case.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears to the man as an Arab and kills him.

terms.meaning: As Rav Huna explains just before, standing outside and facing away while the congregation inside faces the other way, which looks like contempt for the synagogue.
God, before whom one stands in prayer.

17.note: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha recalls that he once entered the innermost sanctum of the Temple to offer incense. He saw Akatriel Ya, the Lord of Hosts, seated on a high and exalted throne, who said: Yishmael, My son, bless Me. He answered: May it be Your will that Your mercy overcome Your anger, that Your mercy prevail over Your other attributes, that You deal with Your children with mercy, and that You go beyond the letter of the law for them. God nodded His head. The Gemara draws the lesson that one should not take even an ordinary person's blessing lightly.
17.why: Rav has just taught, as Rav Zutra bar Tovia reports, that God Himself prays in these very words, asking that His mercy overcome His anger. Rabbi Yishmael's blessing echoes that prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: The High Priest, according to the translation, who enters to offer incense and is asked to bless God.

people.name: Akatriel Ya, the Lord of Hosts
people.about: A name for God; He asks Rabbi Yishmael for a blessing and nods in acceptance.

terms.meaning: The Holy of Holies, the innermost room of the Temple in Jerusalem. The translation adds that the High Priest entered it on Yom Kippur to burn incense.

terms.term: beyond the letter of the law
terms.meaning: Acting more generously than strict justice requires.

18.note: A heretic who lived near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tormented him with challenges about verses of the Bible. One day Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi took a rooster, set it between the legs of his bed and watched it, planning to curse the man when the moment of God's anger came. When that moment came, he was asleep. He concluded that it is not proper to do such a thing, since it is written: His mercy is over all His works.
18.why: Abaye has just said that the moment of God's anger can be known by a rooster: its crest turns white with no red streaks. The story shows a Sage trying to use that sign, and the Gemara adds a verse that punishment is not good even for the righteous.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage who plans to curse his tormentor and falls asleep at the moment he waited for.

terms.meaning: Someone who rejects the Sages' teaching; this one kept challenging Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi over verses.
A brief moment each day when, the discussion says, God is angry, so a curse spoken then might take effect.

19.note: Rav Pappa went to visit an Aramean woman. She brought out a bed and told him to sit. He said he would not sit until she lifted the bedding. She lifted it, and they found a dead baby there. The translation explains that had he sat, he would have been blamed for killing the child. From this the Sages said it is forbidden to sit on an Aramean woman's bed.
19.why: Rava has just advised his sons not to sit on the bed of an Aramean woman, and the Gemara gives three readings of his words. This incident explains the literal reading.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who refuses to sit until the bed is uncovered.

terms.meaning: A non-Jewish woman, as the translation explains.

20.note: A pair of Sages got drunk at the wedding of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's son. The translation explains that they fell asleep before saying the evening Shema and woke after dawn. They came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said: Rabbi Shimon is worthy of being relied on in a pressing situation.
20.why: A ruling had been reported in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name that the law follows Rabbi Shimon, who lets the evening Shema be said just before sunrise. Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef said he never said so outright; it was inferred from this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage at whose son's wedding the two got drunk; they ask him what to do.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The Sage whose lenient view Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lets them rely on.

terms.meaning: The central declaration of faith ('Hear, O Israel'), said each evening and morning within set times.
Under hardship or after the fact. A lenient view relied on only then is not the rule for ordinary cases.
